Because I believe that that kind of declaration will be useful and will in itself be an educating force which can be held up as an example to all the people of Canada, I intend to vote for this bill as it is at the present time.

I think those hon. members who have had training in the law are aware that the common law definition of libel has always been that type of statement which would tend to bring another person into hatred, ridicule or contempt. I know that the special committee under the chairmanship of Dean Cohen, when it presented its recommendations to the then Minister of Justice, the late Hon. I should like to refer the House briefly to the three offences. The first offence is that of advocating or promoting genocide. Existing criminal law in the Code prohibits homicide of an individual person. Whereas I suppose it is conceivable that one could have homicide of a group of people within the existing terms of the law, the bill deems it necessary to create a new offence of advocating or promoting genocide, because there is now no offence in the Code of advocating or promoting the homicide of a group of people. When one turns to the second offence of public incitement of hatred and contempt likely to lead to a breach of the peace, I am advised there is a gap in the law today which derives from the fact that it does not penalize the initiating party who incites to hatred and contempt with a likelihood of violence, whether or not intended and whether or not violence takes place.
An hon. member referred to the case of Boucher v. the King, (1950) 1st DLR at page 267. The burden of that case was that the protection of groups under the provisions of the criminal law extends only to certain situations where a prosecution can prove violence was intended, whether or not the violence was a likely result of the action. The law is based on intention not on a likelihood of result following cause, effect following cause. It is the intention which is considered to be the necessary element under the present law as interpreted by the Boucher case. The third offence, the wilful promotion of hatred, is, again, on the advice I have received, not covered within the present provisions of the Criminal Code. If you turn to those sections of the Code dealing with defamatory libel, commencing with section 248, you will see that there is no specific protection extended to groups. The committee had this to say on the subject:
-the defining words in section 248 preclude any protection for groups-
The reason is, of course, that the defamatory libel must be against the person and not against a group of persons. It is the word "person" that is used in present section 248 of the Code. Of course, the members of a group are still protected as individuals against a libel in collective form, but to establish the publisher's liability it would be necessary for the prosecution to show that the libel exposed every member of the group individually to hatred, contempt or ridicule.
The committee also considered section 166 dealing with the publication of false statements likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest, and section 315(1) penalizing the sending of false information with intent to injure or alarm. Both these sections, in the opinion of the committee, have only very limited application to hate propaganda, for two reasons: first, both require the Crown to prove that the libeller knows that the matter is false. Not only is this a heavy burden for the Crown to meet, but it is undoubtedly true that many purveyors of group libel are sick or misguided men who thoroughly believe in the truth of their statements. Second, both apparently apply only to straight matters of fact and would have no application to any matters of opinion. The committee concluded with these words:
In sum then, it is evident that the Criminal Code, even on the widest interpretation, does little or nothing to protect groups from the evils of hate propaganda.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that there have been philosophic objections to this bill. I want to deal with them as my final point. The philosophic objection to this bill has predicated itself on a certain set of assumptions about the right of free speech in a democratic society. Accordingly, as the argument goes and as the bill's detractors say, the bill infringes on


Hate Propaganda
free speech and arrests the freedom of expression so necessary to a democratic polity.
This kind of verbal gamesmanship is misleading and is based on three hidden but false assumptions. First, it suggests that the arguments in respect of the bill must resolve themselves in terms of whether one is for or against free speech-categorically for or categorically against free speech. Second, it suggests that the right of free speech is an absolute and unfettered right; and third, it questions the validity of the criminal sanction as an educative process. Let me deal with each of these assumptions which form the basis of the philosophic opposition to the bill.
First, I believe one's attitude toward this bill cannot, or should not depend on whether one is for or against free speech. I, of course, believe every hon. member of the House is in favour of free speech, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. One's position respecting the bill cannot be construed as an automatic label of one's civil libertarian position. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has spoken of civil libertarians who are against the bill, but he also spoke with equal authority and experience of civil libertarians who are in favour of the bill. There are respected libertarians who have argued on both sides of this particular piece of legislation. The question is not whether one is for or against free speech but, rather, what are the permissible limits on free speech; what are the permissible contours of freedom of speech and expression?
To put the question another way, to put it in absolute terms and say that if one is for the bill one is against freedom of speech, and if one is against the bill one is for freedom of speech, is to display a type of verbal sleight of hand, a type of verbal gamesmanship. It is what Professor Harold Lasswell of Yale law school has called "the cloud of normative ambiguity", because it derives the normative value by declaring that support of this legislation is tantamount to infringing on freedom of expression and is therefore anti-civil libertarian and even anti-democratic, rather than appreciating the morality of the behaviour being proscribed and the normative value of the principle being affirmed. The principle being affirmed is that no democratic process should oblige any of its members to subject themselves to verbal maiming or lethal language which cannot possibly have any intrinsic redeeming value or advantage, either in 
terms of freedom of speech or the democratic process.
There is a second false assumption on the part of those opposing this bill. I am not saying that the opposition to this bill is not sincere or is not well-founded. I am not being categorical and saying that the bill is a good or bad bill, because when we talk about the subtle balance between freedom of expression on the one hand and the abuse of that freedom by the dissemination of hatred on the other, no one can be absolutely sure or absolutely categorical that he is right. It is a question of value judgment; it is a question of feeling. I submit to Your Honour that the members of the government and the members of the committee who studied this bill tried to achieve a reasonable balance, a reasonable reconciliation, so that the conflicting legitimate interests of freedom of expression on the one hand and the protection of reputation and group identity on the other are balanced. This is a very difficult thing to achieve and we have tried to do our best.
We must realize that nowhere in our constitution and legal practice, and nowhere in our constitutional tradition is there any sanction of the concept of absolute liberty. There is no such thing as an absolute freedom of speech; there is no such thing as an absolute right of assembly. We are dealing with a right which we are trying to enhance without infringing on the rights and privileges of other people. If the hon. member for Calgary North says that the Bill of Rights is impliedly against this piece of legislation, I say that that argument is a bit of sophistry. True, the Bill of Rights talks in terms of freedom of expression, but there is nothing in the Bill of Rights that says there is an absolute freedom of expression.
There is nothing in the constitution of the United States to say that there is an absolute freedom of expression or freedom of assembly. Indeed, no democratic process, Mr. Speaker, could categorically licence any absolute rights-and the hon. member for Winnipeg North pointed out clearly the difference between a right and the abuse of that right by licence-without endangering the viability of the democratic process itself. The history of democratic society is the history of the balancing of legitimate interests and legitimate rights as between various members and classes of that society and between members of that society and the government by which they are governed.


The concept of absolute freedom is a perversion of the rule of law. It is the replacement of the rule of law by the rule of absolutism. The tradition of the enhancement and the enlargement of the right of freedom of expression-the hon. member for Calgary North cited some of the landmarks that have enhanced and enlarged the right of freedom of speech-is part of a parallel process whereby there have been placed at the same time necessary limitations and restrictions on the legitimacy of freedom of speech.
The criminal law of Canada, modelled upon the criminal law of England, authorizes freedom of speech but not in absolute terms. It does so within permissible contours, within permissible parameters. One need only refer to the present rules regarding defamation, blasphemy, sedition, libel or scurrilous material to appreciate the attempt, made throughout the history of Canada and under the rules of the common law, to draw boundaries between what is permissible and what is not permissible speech rather than to speak in terms of freedom of speech in absolute terms. From time immemorial there have been limitations on the freedom of speech and our laws of libel and slander are examples of this.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We are merely broadening, in the main purview of this bill, the law of libel and slander to include group libel and group slander. I have no right to defame my neighbour's reputation. There must be no right to promote the hatred of people on the basis of race or religion, the hatred of people who are distinguishable by colour or by their ethnic origin, let alone advocate their total annihilation or advocate genocide. No democratic process worthy of its name can licence the advocacy of genocide in the name of the democratic process itself. No claim to freedom of speech can legitimate the incitement of racial hatred and condone the breakdown of social order in the name of free speech.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, one must reject the charge that this legislation involves an invalid use of the criminal sanction. Such an objection not only fails, in my submission, to appreciate the intrinsic value of this legislation in respect of outlawing hate propaganda itself, but ignores the educational value of the legal process in general and the criminal sanction in particular. The measure of our laws, it has been said, is the measure of our civilization. If we are to have justice in socie-
Hate Propaganda
ty, then we must begin with just laws. Nowhere is this more important than in the realm of criminal law. It is here that the most fundamental values of life, liberty and dignity are to be protected and sanctioned, and it is here that the measure of our commitment to these values will be tested.
I do not consider the criminal law to be just an agency of social control. I do not consider it to be merely what Herbert Packer called the controlled use of power in society. I consider it to be a set of articulated values by which civilized men tend to regulate their lives and measure their society. That being so, this law will represent part of those articulated values by which we tend to regulate our conduct as free citizens in Canada.
This law is not just a technical body of rules. It tends within the conduct that is prescribed to articulate the values by which we Canadians seek to live. The criminal law is not merely a sanction or control process. It is reflective and declaratory of the moral sense of a community and the total integrity of a community. It seeks not merely to proscribe, but to educate. It seeks to set forth a threshold of tolerance and standards of minimum order and decency.
I echo what many members have said in committee and in this House. One cannot legislate a community to love or even eradicate by legislation the promotion of feelings of hatred. But one can control certain kinds of public hate dissemination and hate activity. One can put this country on record as declaring that the conscience of the Canadian community will not tolerate that kind of activity. One can put the Canadian community on record as subscribing to the international conventions, which other hon. members have referred to, under the auspices of the United Nations.
What this bill hopes and seeks to articulate is that we condemn the social evil of the deliberate, wilful dissemination of racial hatred in this country and elsewhere. We consider it to be a poison in a civilized society. We consider it to be contrary to the collective moral sense and total integrity of the Canadian community. We consider in the global village in which we are living, which is almost claustrophobic, that the exploitation of hostility in man and the skilful promotion of hatred must be combatted. As such, in its ultimate sense the criminal law sanction, and in this context the bill outlawing the dissemination of hate-and I make no prediction as


Hate Propaganda
to how successful this legislation is going to be; I would be a fool to try to do it and so would any other member-is a conscientious attempt on the part of the government, and I hope of Parliament itself, to outlaw as an articulation of the total integrity of the Canadian community the dissemination of hate in this country and throughout the world, proclaiming our commitment to humanity, humanism and to the rule of law.

Mr. Speaker, one would think from the eloquent words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) that feuding, fighting, fussing and inciting to hatred, ridicule, contempt and the like were rampant in the streets of the global village. This measure has been before the other place for two sessions and before us for this session. I have yet to hear any discussions regarding any instances where the thoughts embodies in the bill have any particular application to this country. I am serious: I have yet to hear where it has any application to this country.
I know we receive in our mailboxes publications from the two opposing sides dealing with events that are taking place 5,000 miles to the east. I suppose those reports that we receive are the communication of statements which are supposed to incite our hatred of an identifiable group which is likely to lead to a breach of the peace, yet I have not heard of these groups seriously coming to blows with each other. I have not heard that these publications, which might be deemed to wilfully promote hatred, have led to any serious disturbance in Canada. They probably led to a discussion or some process of thoughts in our own minds as to whether we should take one side or the other or, sensibly as Canadians, we should try to find a mutual way to resolve a dispute in some other part of the world that, if not resolved, could lead us into disaster. In short, propound with regard to Bill C-3 what I call the Hatfield and McCoy theory, that we have not seen that feud transferred to Canada. If we are not using atomic weapons, we are using a great deal of parliamentary puff to try to dispel things that largely do not exist. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am very sceptical. It remains to be proven to me during this debate that the exercise we are going through is meaningful.
I can agree with the first part of the formula in Bill C-3 without any difficulty. I think it should probably be passed in about five minutes without anybody giving too IMr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton).]
much attention to it. I do not think anyone in Canada would advocate or promote genocide. However, if a person, short of the lunatic stage, is inclined to promote genocide in Canada, we must deal with him or her promptly. I have my doubts about the purpose of Bill C-3. I know it is the pet child of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The foundling has found its way into the lap of the Minister of Justice. The hon. gentleman is doing the best he can with it. He very properly raised it for a parliamentary blessing, but still I have my doubts.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
This seems to be a bill dealing with thought. It is really an attempt to exercise control over the process of thought, imposing criminal sanctions against thought rather than against action. Most of our Criminal Code deals with actions by one person against another. But look at what is contained here in section 267B: the key words are "communicating statements which incite hatred against any identifiable group where such incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace." First, one has to assess what is meant by the communication of a statement and then somebody has to decide whether the mere fact of such a communication is an incitement to violent action. Finally, one has to determine whether it is likely to lead to a breach of the peace.
Outside this chamber we have all been subjected in the last year to an unusual number of jokes dealing with Newfoundlanders. To most of us who do not have the benefit of coming from that island they may seem very funny. Even if we are close to it, they may seem funny. Though I have never seen a Newfoundlander take exception to these jokes, they may seem less amusing to those directly concerned.
At one time the vogue was for Polish stories. Then it was Italian stories, or Indian stories, or black stories, or something. Is this sort of thing a communication of hatred, or ridicule, or contempt? Is it something designed to bring about a donnybrook? Is it something designed to bring about a belly-laugh? I suppose it would depend upon the circumstances-whether one told the story in a pub in St. John's at midnight or whether one told it somewhere in Alberta. Do we, by telling these stories, communicate hatred, ridicule or contempt? What happens when people tell these strories against themselves? I suggest a jury could look at such statements


and reach entirely different conclusions in different parts of Canada.
Perhaps I have belaboured this point more than it should be belaboured. The point I am trying to make is that a thought expressed in one part of Canada might be taken to mean something entirely different in another part of Canada. This is why it is dangerous to attempt to deal, as I think this bill does, with what would essentially be thought-crimes. A person expressing a certain opinion may well do so for reasons which have nothing to do with inciting a breach of the peace. He may have said those things with his tongue in his cheek. Yet the result could still be a donny-brook, it could be a belly-laugh, or it could merely lead to people saying, "Go away. Don't disturb us with that kind of nonsense. We know you are full of hot air." This is what any of these so-called crimes could, in effect, amount to, depending on the circumstances of utterance. For example, what is said over television today or on the radio today produces an effect far different from that which have been produced by the same statements a hundred years ago. This is why we must proceed very carefully when we deal with the sort of crimes we are trying to establish under 267B. I realize the Attorney General will have to give consent before a prosecution is allowed, but an Attorney General in one part of Canada may have a conception of what constitutes social rectitude entirely different from that held by his counterpart in another province.
Reduced to its essentials, the bill is really dealing not with defamation, libel or slander as between individuals, but with defamation, libel or slander as between classes. It affords an opportunity for one minority, group to say that another minority group is out to get it, or it provides an opportunity for a majority group to complain about a minority group, or for a minority group to complain about majority groups.
Perhaps I am especially sensitive to this issue because recently in Halifax we were visted by an encounter team, experts from outside in sociology, psychology, racial relationships and the like, who turned our community inside out, if I may use that phrase. They examined everything. They lifted the lids from our ids. They wanted to see what made the Halifax area tick-how the black people got along with the white people, and vice versa. They criticized all our methods of government and, in short, they examined everything that could be put out publicly on
Hate Propaganda
the line. In addition, there was the question of the appointment of a city manager.
The gentleman who was chosen by the Halifax city council came from Oklahoma City. At one time he was engaged in labour relations with a certain union. All did not go well, I gather, in his dealings with that union, so people who resented the loss of a victory, in other words, the defeat of the labour union, were quick to telephone Halifax and suggest that the man chosen by the city council to be the city manager was a racist. I think this is germane to the bill, because what happened next was that certain people drew ranks together, just as any rallying crowd would do. There was a tremendous fuss at city hall and the man withdrew his candidacy for city manager of the city that I, along with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), represent in Parliament.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, this happened without the man's true nature being known to the people of Halifax, without there being one word in the charge being made against him of racism, or implied racism-a pretty serious charge if proven. He might have his remedy in the courts, I do not know; but he will have his remedy in public opinion when at some time or other people have the chance to dig out the facts and find out what it was all about. As for the job itself, his salary would have been an increase over what he received in Oklahoma City, and this he will not have thanks to a few who were able to raise the cry of hatred against him. Knowing this man's circumstances and his plight, I sympathize with him. I think he was kicked like a dog and never had his day in regard to public opinion as a result of the vapid thinking of a racist, rallying group, a small minority that nevertheless had its way in my own city.
Despite this, I do not think I could espouse the principle that is contained in a bill such as this. I do not think you can settle a miserable battle in this way, where one man's thoughts or one group's thoughts communicate statements that incite hatred or wilfully promote hatred against another person or another identifiable group. I do not think this situation can be solved by criminal action. You cannot solve this kind of miserable battle in court; it cannot be done in that way.
The only way you can solve battles like this, I think, is to dredge the slugs, the people who espouse hatred or contempt of others,


Hate Propaganda
out from under the rocks and hold them up high where the public can look at them and ask questions. I think essentially they are suffering from sick or misguided minds; perhaps they have infantile minds and are not able to see the whole world as it exists but rather see only their own small part of it.
Every member of the House has received letters in his mailbox, as I have in mine, from someone who dislikes French Canada, from others who dislike English Canada, letters complaining that the Indians are not getting a good break, that the blacks are being hounded, that the WASPs are an ugly bunch, and so on and so forth. We all receive letters like this. If they are all put together, what they add up to is that just about everybody in Canada is a person who should be hated, who should be the object of ridicule and contempt.
This is the way life is. I do not see how we solve these things by having a few brisk court cases-miserable battles, as I called them earlier. I think we are better off having the full spotlight focused upon these situations in a democratic country. These things should be explored in the newspapers, on television and radio. Let us talk about them in Parliament, though perhaps the most distasteful debates that take place in this House are those that deal with human rights. It is always difficult in a political forum to deal with such issues. For example, a few years ago I do not think I made any great contribution to the debate on the Bill of Rights. I went back to it, and this is one of the items I wish I had not talked about, because I think I had some political motivation in getting after certain of my friends who now sit to my left.
Be that as it may, I think it is public discussion and public spotlighting that provides a better answer. The light of truth can be made to shine. People who have to lurk in small corners with their own small prejudices, their own small hates and their own small contempts can be made to live harmlessly from the rest of us. So, Mr. Speaker, unless I am persuaded very much otherwise during the debate tomorrow, I am afraid I cannot accept the principles contained within section 267B (1) and 267B (2), and will support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

Mr. Speaker, in the course of his speech the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) inferred that Bill C-3 is designed for election purposes. I believe he 
has missed the point. The bill before the House is designed to protect minorities, not majorities. Surely this is not a narrow, electioneering purpose. The hon. member has, of course, had little opportunity in recent years to acquire an accurate understanding of majority opinion. He and his party are obviously out of touch with majority opinion in Canada. We are dealing with the dignity of man, and we intend to protect the victims of slanderous prejudice in modem Canadian society. If we pass wise and just laws, we are far more likely to be re-elected than if we retreat and shrink from laws which dignify man in Canadian society.
In speaking against the amendment, I believe that should the amendment pass we would eliminate the direct causes of genocide by criminal restraint. I believe that the House has the courage and the strength actively to prevent abusive, prejudicial expressions of hatred against identifiable minority groups. We agreed through action at the United Nations to take steps to eliminate racial prejudice. This we said and this we shall do. This is why we are here today. We are in the act of doing what is required to equalize the rights of those minority groups, thus giving them the protection they deserve. The high standard set by Canadian justice will be reached by goals such as those contained within the bill. Prejudice will be thwarted by law and by education.
May I call it ten o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, on March 6, not knowing at the time that I was so prophetic in the import of my question, I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), as reported at page 4469 of Hansard:
-what other minister or ministers will now be assigned the duty of bringing about a solution to the prolonged postal dispute in Montreal?
Alas, sir, that prolonged dispute is still facing the country, and the acerbity of the problem has not diminished. Although I asked the question on March 6, the problem began much earlier, on February 3. To say that the Postmaster General is disaster prone is to use


an euphemism. There has been more trouble, more divisiveness and more unrest than in any equal period of any of his predecessors since the great Sir John A. Macdonald occupied the post for one day over 100 years ago.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
One of the kindest things one could say is that the hon. gentleman is a trouble-prone Postmaster General. In this, the most brittle and most bitter of disputes, the government has moved to bail him out and share with him the responsibility for the brittleness, ineptitude, harshness of attitude and lack of perception of the problems. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) today is, unique among the cabinet ministers, away in the cool waters of the Azores. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) is not with us. What he thinks I am not able to divine, but I have my suspicions.
So after many, many weeks of faltering, inadequate or non-service we have an eleventh hour effort to bail out the government and an urgent last minute summons to a man heretofore with an unblemished record, Mr. Goldenberg. Yet this man's report is anything but a paean of praise for the Postmaster General. Indeed, it looks like a carefully documented denunciation and denigration of that hon. gentleman whose activities as Postmaster General some of us have questioned rather stringently and severely in these past many months. Almost, sir, it is as harsh as the denunciation of Mr. Martin of the Public Service Commission some months ago. Significant among the comments of Mr. Goldenberg is that in respect of the moral responsibility of the government in its role as employer. I submit in all the tangled web of uncertainty and misunderstanding that the role of the government as an employer is the very, very significant question we as legislators must face.
Surely the government should be pre-eminent in the realm of labour-management relations and should as an employer be above reproach. But it would be a reckless man who would suggest that in this tangled web of uncertainty, of deception and of regrettable faltering the government has been above reproach. I will pass by quickly Commissioner Goldenberg's comment upon the substitution of the six-day week for the five-day week, a matter upon which many of us have commented, lo these many months, to no avail. But after months of inefficiency, ineptitude and internecine conflict the Post Office has

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion reached a state of paralysis or worse in the most important receiving and distributing centre in our whole nation, namely, the city of Montreal. The failure to give good service to the Canadian people is appalling; but it is something to which the Canadian people should have grown accustomed. But the fact that bad service is tolerable cannot pardon the government for providing no service.
If I had time in these seven minutes I would quote from the illustrious paper, the Ottawa Citizen, the lead editorial which is capitalized "A Catalogue of Blunders." In considering everything, I ask how many more privations the Canadian public must endure in this unseemly conflict between an arrogant Postmaster General and a legitimate union. I am not going to talk about the reported turbulence in the cabinet which it would seem is even more disturbing than the turbulence in some areas of the postal service. It is not my purpose to seek to pry into the workings of the Privy Council to ask who is on slippery slopes or in cold water, but I ask: Are we to punish hundreds of decent, honourable workers who have served the mail service well, in order to follow a certain formula acceptable to a minister or to this government which is not acceptable to the union or to a majority of the cabinet?

Mr. Speaker, on March 12 I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) what plans he had to protect the consumer from a growing pollution menace, that of non-returnable bottles. This is a completely unnecessary evil thrust upon the long suffering consumer by the glass industry. Always on the lookout for expanding markets, they have seized upon the one-trip bottle as the glass industry's bonanza, regardless of the added cost to the consumer, regardless of the danger of broken glass on playgrounds, streets and highways, regardless of the unsightly litter of disgarded bottles everywhere and the difficulties and expense to municipalities of cleaning up the mess.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Such callous disregard for consumer interests has begun to stir community groups into 
action. Organizations such as the Consumer Association of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, the Home and School Association, known in some parts of Canada as the Parent-Teacher Federation, and other large organizations have protested vigorously at their national conventions and have demanded action-so far in vain.
More recently the minister of highways of the province of Alberta declared that unless the federal Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs places a ban on non-returnable bottles, the highways ministers of all ten provinces will discuss ways and means of dealing with this problem. Still more recently the province of British Columbia passed Bill No. 33, the litter Act, section 3 of which reads:
No person shall sell or offer for sale beer, ale, carbonated beverages or drinks in a glass, plastic, or metal container for consumption or use off the premises of which they are sold or offered for sale unless the person undertakes to refund to the purchaser on delivery up of the container the sum of not less than two cents for each container.
This is the sort of legislation we need federally. At the beginning of the tourist season we scarcely need to be reminded of the vast quantities of soft drinks and their containers that will be bought this summer. Will this mean pleasure all around, or will it mean momentary pleasure for the individual and long drawn-out, pain-in-the-neck pollution for the community? Surely we have had enough of pollution without letting this kind of pollution proliferate in the way it is doing. It is up to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; let him ban the one-trip bottle now; let him find ways and means of doing it.
In the days gone by the minister might have been tempted to shelve such action by saying it was strictly provincial in scope. But after the answer he gave through his parliamentary secretary to my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman), on October 3, 1968, no such escape is possible. On that occasion his parliamentary secretary said-I am glad the parliamentary secretary is in the chamber tonight-as follows: However, Mr. Speaker, in line with the minister's duty to promote and encourage the institution of practices tending to improve protection of the Canadian consumer and to co-operate with provincial governments or their agencies, or with private groups, the minister will be having further talks with his officials and will consider the question of non-returnable bottles, with a view to formulating some type of regulation.
After these departmental talks, it is intended to invite representatives of the manufacturers, the user and the retail distributors of these bottles to
April 6, 1970	COMMONS
Ottawa to discuss the problems and all proposals, as well as ascertain from these people what they intend to do relative to the problem mentioned by the hon. member.
I repeat that that was on October 3, 1968. After 18 months, Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting to hear the result of these talks, formulations, invitations, discussions, ascertainments, intentions-I take all that language from the reply-and what-nots, and that last expression is my own, on non-returnable bottles, which is the problem we are talking about.
Non-returnable bottles are to be found everywhere. The retailer does not care what happens after the sale is made. The empties will be found in householder garbage cans, in parks, rivers and lakes, on lawns, streets, in roadside ditches and even in grain fields. Some of us remember the Russian wheat deal and how the Russians could not handle the grain because of the broken-bottle litter in it. How about watching out for our export trade, because it is important. Non-returnable bottles can be a great factor in making more accidents possible, and damage and injuries greater. Death can be accelerated by contact with broken glass carelessly thrown in a ditch after a minor car accident.
After all these prolonged negotiations we are waiting to hear what the minister has come up with, after he has invited the provinces, the glass people, the consumers and the retailers and everybody else to Ottawa to do all this discussing. Surely after 18 months he is beginning to come up with something to protect the consumer. Pollution is a thorny problem with many ugly angles. Few are uglier or more unsightly than the broken glass which wastes our resources, endangers our children and infests our landscape. Again I ask the minister, what plans has he to deal with this pollution menace?
Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) I would first like to assure all hon. members of the House that the department is not only concerned about the problem of nonreturnable bottles but also is giving this problem very urgent consideration. In particular, the department is now looking into standards for containers. In general, I should like to say that we are very much aware of at least two major problems presented by non-returnable bottles, the problem of litter and the problem of safety.

It has been suggested frequently that the federal government ban the sale of beverages in non-returnable bottles. I should like to emphasize that the federal Parliament has jurisdiction only over that part of trade and commerce which is interprovincial or international. Since soft drinks and beer enter interprovincial trade rarely, if at all, any action by the federal Parliament would be ineffective in dealing with the problem. Any legislation to ban the sale of beverages in disposable bottles would have to be passed by the provincial legislatures.
Non-returnable bottles are only one cause of the litter created by containers. Legislation to prevent the use of non-returnable bottles would be only a partial remedy. The hon. member has already mentioned the Litter Act which was introduced into the legislature of British Columbia and which will be under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Recreation and Conservation. I should like to commend the government of British Columbia for introducing such a bill, one which defines litter by including rubbish, garbage, waste material, containers, packages, bottles, cans or parts thereof. The hon. member has already mentioned section 3, about the refund that should be made to the purchaser, and other sections of this act. It is one which I believe should be commended to all provinces of Canada, Mr. Speaker. This bill will require that all containers for beverages be returnable and will prohibit the littering of waters and lands, the spoiling and fouling of waters and adjacent land.
Mr. Speaker, this is all I can say at the present time, but I have made note of the representations made by the hon. member and I should like to assure her that I will bring this matter to the attention of the minister.

Mr. Speaker, the decision of Mr. Justice Craig Munroe with regard to the rather unique method by which the government proclaimed the breathalyzer provision of the amendments to the Criminal Code was not the first time this matter had been raised publicly. On January 15, in this House of Commons, at page 2464 of Hansard, at just about this time of day I said:
I note that it has been accepted over the years that certain sections of acts can be proclaimed, and indeed have been proclaimed, without the whole


Proceedings on Adjournment Motion body of the act being proclaimed at one time. But I have never heard of a package within an act being proclaimed and little snippets and pieces of that package being cut out and held up until a future proclamation.
My understanding that this was a very unusual course was reinforced when I spoke to two members of the class of 1940 in the House, the righit hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In their vast parliamentary experience-and nobody is their equal in that regard -they could not recall such a course being adopted.
I made that statement then, nobody has challenged me since, and I stand by it. I think on behalf of Parliament a big vote of thanks is due Mr. Justice Craig Munroe for doing what we should be able to do but find ourselves powerless to do once the government acts in such an unusual fashion.
